mall: Every star you win in a mission pays for one piece of a landmark.
Let’s rebuild the National Mall, starting with the Washington Monument.
You rebuilt the whole Mall, from the Lincoln Memorial to the Capitol.
Every piece was paid for with stars you earned.
The tall marble obelisk in the middle of the Mall, for the first president.
Finished in 1884 and just over 555 feet tall, it was the tallest structure in the world until the Eiffel Tower, in 1889.
Here’s your Mall so far.
Next up: the Washington Monument.
The monument stands a little south and east of the spot first planned for it: the ground there was swampy and unstable.
The cornerstone was laid on July 4, 1848.
Work stopped in 1854 at about 152 feet, when the Washington National Monument Society ran out of money.
It stood unfinished through the Civil War.
In 1878 the Army Corps of Engineers took over, and first made the foundation stronger.
The new marble came from a different quarry, so you can still see the color change about 150 feet up.
The pointed top is a marble pyramid 55 feet tall, set on a shaft 500 feet tall.
On December 6, 1884, workers set the capstone, tipped with a small pyramid of solid aluminum weighing 100 ounces.
Fifty U.S flags fly in a circle around the base, for the fifty states.
The Greek temple at the west end of the Mall, with the Reflecting Pool in front.
The memorial was dedicated on May 30, 1922.
Next up: the Lincoln Memorial.
The memorial stands on land the Army Corps of Engineers built up from Potomac River mud flats.
Its foundations reach bedrock 44 to 65 feet down.
Architect Henry Bacon designed the memorial.
Ground was broken on February 12, 1914, Lincoln’s birthday.
There are 36 columns, one for each state in the Union when Lincoln died.
All 36 columns are up.
The frieze above them carries the names of those 36 states.
Higher up, the attic carries the names of the 48 states of 1922, the year the memorial was dedicated.
Daniel Chester French designed the statue, and the Piccirilli brothers carved it from 28 blocks of white Georgia marble.
It is 19 feet tall.
The Reflecting Pool, finished in 1924, stretches about 2,000 feet east toward the Washington Monument.
At night the memorial is lit up at the end of the pool.
The round, domed memorial on the Tidal Basin, south of the Washington Monument.
Words from the Declaration of Independence are carved on its inside walls.
Next up: the Jefferson Memorial.
The memorial stands on the south bank of the Tidal Basin, in a straight line with the White House to the north.
Part of the basin was filled in to line it up.
Its ring has 26 columns.
John Russell Pope’s design follows the Pantheon in Rome, which also shaped Jefferson’s own Monticello and the University of Virginia Rotunda.
President Franklin Roosevelt laid the cornerstone on November 15, 1939.
The memorial was dedicated on April 13, 1943, Jefferson’s 200th birthday.
During the war, metal was scarce, so a plaster statue painted the color of bronze stood here first.
The 19-foot bronze went in in 1947.
The cherry trees around the Tidal Basin were a gift of about 3,000 trees from the city of Tokyo.
The first two were planted in 1912.
Next door to the White House: the home of the Department of the Treasury, which collects and pays the government’s money.
It is the oldest departmental building in Washington, built in stages from 1836 to 1869.
Next up: the Treasury Building.
The building went up in stages, starting in 1836 with the east and center wings, designed by Robert Mills.
The east front, on 15th Street, has 30 granite columns, each 36 feet tall and cut from a single block.
The south, west and north wings followed, one after another.
The north wing, the last, was finished in 1869, more than thirty years after the first stone.
This is where the money of the federal government is managed: taxes coming in, bills going out, and the debt.
A statue of Alexander Hamilton, the first Secretary of the Treasury, stands on the south plaza.
It was dedicated in 1923.
The president’s house, north of the Washington Monument, where each year’s budget request begins.
Every president since John Adams has lived here.

James Hoban designed the house.
The cornerstone was laid on October 13, 1792.
In 1798 the sandstone walls got a coat of lime whitewash, to protect them.
The name White House stuck, and in 1901 Theodore Roosevelt made it official.
John Adams was the first president to live here, starting on November 1, 1800.
British troops burned the house in August 1814, during the War of 1812.
James Hoban rebuilt it in a little less than three years.
The round South Portico, with its columns, was added in 1824.
Each year the president sends Congress a budget request: the first step toward a federal budget.
A fountain plays on the South Lawn, in front of the portico.
Congress’s home, at the east end of the Mall, where every federal dollar is approved.
Every federal dollar spent, and every tax collected, starts as a bill passed here.

George Washington laid the cornerstone on September 18, 1793.
The design was by William Thornton.
Congress first met here on November 17, 1800, in the north wing, then the only part finished.
It held the Senate, the House, the Supreme Court and the Library of Congress.
The House moved into its new chamber in the south wing in 1807.
British troops burned the Capitol in 1814.
Charles Bulfinch finished the rebuilt center in 1826, under a low wooden dome covered in copper.
Congress grew with the country and outgrew its rooms.

The old dome came down, and a new one of cast iron went up in its place, starting in 1855.

Work went on through the Civil War; Lincoln called it a sign that the Union would go on.
The Statue of Freedom, by Thomas Crawford, was set on top of the dome on December 2, 1863.
Philip Reid, an enslaved worker at the foundry, worked out how to take apart its plaster model so it could be cast in bronze.
